analysis.one_liner: Taxes large AI companies to fund public-service jobs with wage and union protections.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in August 2026 with three Democratic cosponsors, sits in two House committees with no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill puts a small excise tax on companies that build or sell access to large 'foundation' AI models, based on the value of the AI activity they process or sell, and it sets a higher rate when unemployment rises. The money goes into a trust fund for a new Work Protection Administration at the Labor Department, which would hand out competitive grants to states, cities, schools, and nonprofits to hire people for public-service work — child care, tutoring, health outreach, elder care, housing repair, infrastructure, local news, and more. Those grant-funded jobs must pay at least the local prevailing or minimum wage, include federal-employee-style health coverage, paid leave, and paid family leave, and honor workers' rights to organize. The bill also directs the Bureau of Labor Statistics to track how AI is displacing or degrading jobs, and allows up to 20 percent of the fund for existing workforce training programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and communities served by the new jobs: people hired into child care, schools, health care, elder care, housing repair, infrastructure, and local journalism positions with wage floors, health coverage, and paid leave. Grant recipients such as state and local governments, public schools, and nonprofits gain hiring money, and unions gain because grant-funded employers must post labor-rights notices and recognize a union chosen by a majority of the affected workers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers, unions, and local public services

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an excise tax on AI foundation model companies equal to roughly 2 percent of the value of tokens they process or 3 percent of AI revenue, rising automatically as unemployment climbs above 5 percent, with the rate doubling its increase above 7 percent.
Deposits 100 percent of the tax into a trust fund dedicated to a Labor Department jobs program, so the revenue is earmarked rather than going to general spending.

Funds competitive grants to states, cities, tribal governments, public schools, and nonprofits to hire people for jobs in child care, education support, public health, elder and disability care, housing construction and rehabilitation, homelessness services, public safety, infrastructure, parks, local news, and workforce training.

Requires every grant-funded job to pay at least the highest of federal or state minimum wage or the local prevailing wage, include health coverage comparable to federal employees' plan, twelve weeks of paid family and medical leave, and one hour of paid leave per 30 hours worked.

Bars grant recipients from using the money to replace laid-off workers, take strikers' jobs, or displace existing staff's hours or pay, and requires employers to recognize a union if a majority of the affected employees want one.

Directs the Bureau of Labor Statistics to measure AI's effects on the workforce, including job degradation such as lower pay, fewer hours, and job insecurity, with $20 million a year authorized for that work through fiscal 2031.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that develop, sell access to, or internally use large AI foundation models — especially where that use reduces their own or a related company's workforce — pay the excise tax. Some of that cost could be passed through to businesses and consumers who use AI services. Government and university research uses are exempt.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large AI model developers and their customers

drawbacks.text: Because the tax is levied on companies that sell AI access, some of the cost would likely be passed through to prices for businesses and consumers who use AI services.

The bill asks the Treasury Secretary to determine the 'fair market value' of an individual token, an unprecedented valuation exercise, and covers companies that merely modify an existing open-weight model, which raises compliance questions about how the tax applies across the fast-changing AI industry.

The tax rate is tied to the highest unemployment rate of the prior three years, measured on a broad definition that counts discouraged and part-time-for-economic-reasons workers, so rates could stay elevated long after a downturn ends, though the Secretary may suspend the increase if unemployment rose from a war, pandemic, or other shock unrelated to AI.

The jobs program is funded only 'subject to the availability of funds' in the trust fund, so the promised jobs depend entirely on the tax raising money, and eligible grant recipients are limited to governments, schools, and nonprofits, not private employers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs a modest new tax on a concentrated, fast-growing industry with a large, concrete jobs and safety-net program, and its labor standards (prevailing wages, health coverage, paid leave, nondisplacement, union recognition) are stronger than typical grant programs. The honest tradeoffs are on the other side: passing a new tax through to AI customers, unusual and hard-to-administer tax definitions, an unemployment trigger that could keep rates high after a downturn, and jobs that exist only as long as the tax collects revenue. It is an ambitious design that would need careful Treasury and Labor implementation to work as written.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 2026 and referred to the House Education and Workforce and Ways and Means committees, where it has sat without any hearing, markup, or vote since.

narrative.text: Representative Greg Casar introduced the bill in the House on August 6, 2026, joined by Representatives Foushee and Jacobs.
The Speaker referred it to the Committee on Education and Workforce and to the Committee on Ways and Means, which would handle the jobs program and the tax provisions respectively.
Three of 217 House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.
The action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action in the months since referral, with the 119th Congress still in session.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, AI companies and other firms that would owe the tax, because the bill has not advanced and no committee has acted on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: AI companies, so far — the bill has not advanced

sides.party_line_note: No vote has been taken, so there is no roll call to read; all support so far is Democratic (the sponsor and three cosponsors, none Republican), and the Republican-controlled committees that hold the bill have taken no action.

industries.industry: AI foundation model developers and sellers
industries.note: The bill taxes roughly 2 percent of the value of AI tokens processed or 3 percent of AI revenue for large foundation model companies, with higher rates when unemployment is elevated, and explicitly taxes internal company use of AI that reduces that company's workforce. Its premise is that the money AI firms would otherwise save by cutting jobs should fund replacement employment for the workers affected.

Any employer hiring with grant funds must post workers' NLRA rights, not discourage organizing, and recognize a union chosen by a majority of the affected employees — making the jobs program a source of union-represented employment.

industries.industry: State and local governments, public schools, and nonprofits (grant recipients)
industries.note: They would receive competitive federal funding to hire workers for child care, education, health, elder care, housing, infrastructure, and local news work — services they currently struggle to staff. Public-sector and nonprofit services would grow at no direct cost to them.

analysis.trajectory: With no action in the months since referral, three cosponsors, and a narrow Republican House majority, the bill is very unlikely to get a hearing or a floor vote in this Congress; it would need committee chairs in both chambers to schedule work that has not begun.
